title: Heart Failure — Mechanisms & Drug Treatment
moduleName: Medical Physiology, Research Methods and Skills

cards.explanation: It is a syndrome with different underlying causes, not a single structural lesion.
cards.text: Heart failure involves cardiac output inadequate to meet the body’s {{c1::metabolic demands}}.
cards.question: Heart failure involves cardiac output inadequate to meet the body’s {{c1::metabolic demands}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture contrasts this with progressive chronic failure.
cards.text: An infarct can precipitate {{c1::acute}} heart failure through sudden loss of cardiac function.
cards.question: An infarct can precipitate {{c1::acute}} heart failure through sudden loss of cardiac function.

cards.explanation: The lecture contrasts this with impaired relaxation or compliance in diastolic failure.
cards.text: Systolic failure is characterised primarily by impaired {{c1::contractility}}.
cards.question: Systolic failure is characterised primarily by impaired {{c1::contractility}}.

cards.explanation: Contractility may be preserved, so preserved ejection fraction does not exclude heart failure.
cards.text: Diastolic failure reduces ventricular filling through impaired relaxation or reduced {{c1::compliance}}.
cards.question: Diastolic failure reduces ventricular filling through impaired relaxation or reduced {{c1::compliance}}.

cards.explanation: EF = (EDV − ESV) / EDV × 100%; the slide asks for this definition.
cards.text: Ejection fraction is stroke volume divided by {{c1::end-diastolic volume}}.
cards.question: Ejection fraction is stroke volume divided by {{c1::end-diastolic volume}}.

cards.explanation: Worked application of the EF definition: (150−90)/150 ×100. These numbers are a revision example, not patient data.
cards.text: A ventricle with EDV 150 mL and ESV 90 mL has an ejection fraction of {{c1::40%}}.
cards.question: A ventricle with EDV 150 mL and ESV 90 mL has an ejection fraction of {{c1::40%}}.

cards.explanation: It uses <40% as its teaching cut-off. Contemporary classifications also recognise HFmrEF; avoid treating the slide’s two-column table as exhaustive.
cards.text: The lecture’s HFrEF example has a {{c1::reduced ejection fraction}}.
cards.question: The lecture’s HFrEF example has a {{c1::reduced ejection fraction}}.

cards.explanation: A stiff ventricle may fill poorly while ejecting a preserved proportion of its filled volume.
cards.text: HFpEF can occur despite a {{c1::preserved ejection fraction}}.
cards.question: HFpEF can occur despite a {{c1::preserved ejection fraction}}.

cards.explanation: The table gives typical patterns, not requirements in every individual.
cards.text: A dilated cavity and increased end-systolic volume fit the lecture’s {{c1::systolic failure}} pattern.
cards.question: A dilated cavity and increased end-systolic volume fit the lecture’s {{c1::systolic failure}} pattern.

cards.explanation: A preserved EF therefore does not imply normal filling pressure.
cards.text: Raised ventricular end-diastolic pressure can occur in {{c1::both systolic and diastolic failure}}.
cards.question: Raised ventricular end-diastolic pressure can occur in {{c1::both systolic and diastolic failure}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture table uses <40%; this clarification includes the conventional boundary and does not establish HF from EF alone.
cards.text: The usual modern HFrEF boundary is an EF of {{c1::40% or less}}.
cards.question: The usual modern HFrEF boundary is an EF of {{c1::40% or less}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture writes >50%; a preserved EF alone is not enough to diagnose HFpEF.
cards.text: The usual modern HFpEF EF range begins at {{c1::50%}}.
cards.question: The usual modern HFpEF EF range begins at {{c1::50%}}.

cards.explanation: Increased pulmonary venous/capillary pressure favours oedema.
cards.text: Raised left-sided filling pressures transmit backwards into the {{c1::pulmonary circulation}}.
cards.question: Raised left-sided filling pressures transmit backwards into the {{c1::pulmonary circulation}}.

cards.explanation: The consequence is peripheral rather than primarily pulmonary congestion.
cards.text: Right ventricular failure produces backward congestion of {{c1::systemic veins}}.
cards.question: Right ventricular failure produces backward congestion of {{c1::systemic veins}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture also lists cough, frothy sputum and rales; these signs are not individually diagnostic.
cards.text: Pulmonary oedema impairs gas exchange and contributes to {{c1::dyspnoea}}.
cards.question: Pulmonary oedema impairs gas exchange and contributes to {{c1::dyspnoea}}.

cards.explanation: It is listed among symptoms associated with pulmonary congestion.
cards.text: Breathlessness when lying flat is called {{c1::orthopnoea}}.
cards.question: Breathlessness when lying flat is called {{c1::orthopnoea}}.

cards.explanation: Right-sided failure can also congest the liver and gastrointestinal tract.
cards.text: Dependent ankle oedema and ascites are examples of {{c1::systemic venous congestion}}.
cards.question: Dependent ankle oedema and ascites are examples of {{c1::systemic venous congestion}}.

cards.explanation: Fatigue, exercise intolerance and renal dysfunction may follow; this differs from the backward congestion pathway.
cards.text: Reduced forward cardiac output causes inadequate {{c1::tissue perfusion}}.
cards.question: Reduced forward cardiac output causes inadequate {{c1::tissue perfusion}}.

cards.explanation: ADH, natriuretic peptides and cardiac remodelling are also included in the lecture.
cards.text: A fall in output and blood pressure activates the sympathetic system and {{c1::RAAS}}.
cards.question: A fall in output and blood pressure activates the sympathetic system and {{c1::RAAS}}.

cards.explanation: This initially helps maintain output, but persistent activation can increase demand and arrhythmias.
cards.text: Short-term sympathetic activation increases heart rate and {{c1::contractility}}.
cards.question: Short-term sympathetic activation increases heart rate and {{c1::contractility}}.

cards.explanation: A compensatory response can therefore worsen the workload of the failing ventricle.
cards.text: Persistent sympathetic vasoconstriction increases ventricular {{c1::afterload}}.
cards.question: Persistent sympathetic vasoconstriction increases ventricular {{c1::afterload}}.

cards.explanation: Excess retention contributes to pulmonary or peripheral oedema.
cards.text: RAAS and ADH promote fluid retention, increasing blood volume and {{c1::preload}}.
cards.question: RAAS and ADH promote fluid retention, increasing blood volume and {{c1::preload}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture contrasts a thickened, poorly filling heart with dilatation and impaired contraction.
cards.text: Excessive ventricular hypertrophy may reduce filling by increasing {{c1::stiffness}}.
cards.question: Excessive ventricular hypertrophy may reduce filling by increasing {{c1::stiffness}}.

cards.explanation: Their renal actions counter fluid retention.
cards.text: ANP and BNP promote excretion of sodium and {{c1::water}}.
cards.question: ANP and BNP promote excretion of sodium and {{c1::water}}.

cards.explanation: They also inhibit renin release, opposing some RAAS effects.
cards.text: ANP and BNP cause {{c1::vasodilation}}.
cards.question: ANP and BNP cause {{c1::vasodilation}}.

cards.explanation: BNP is B-type natriuretic peptide.
cards.text: ANP stands for {{c1::atrial natriuretic peptide}}.
cards.question: ANP stands for {{c1::atrial natriuretic peptide}}.

cards.explanation: Greater end-diastolic stretch normally strengthens contraction.
cards.text: The Frank–Starling relationship links increased filling to increased {{c1::stroke volume}}.
cards.question: The Frank–Starling relationship links increased filling to increased {{c1::stroke volume}}.

cards.explanation: Larger increases in filling then produce only small gains in stroke volume, with greater congestion risk.
cards.text: Reduced contractility shifts the stroke-volume–EDV curve {{c1::downwards}}.
cards.question: Reduced contractility shifts the stroke-volume–EDV curve {{c1::downwards}}.

cards.explanation: This is the class description in the visual table.
cards.text: No limitation with ordinary physical activity corresponds to {{c1::NYHA class I}}.
cards.question: No limitation with ordinary physical activity corresponds to {{c1::NYHA class I}}.

cards.explanation: The table describes a slight limitation of activity.
cards.text: Symptoms with ordinary activity but comfort at rest correspond to {{c1::NYHA class II}}.
cards.question: Symptoms with ordinary activity but comfort at rest correspond to {{c1::NYHA class II}}.

cards.explanation: The table describes marked limitation.
cards.text: Symptoms with less-than-ordinary activity but comfort at rest correspond to {{c1::NYHA class III}}.
cards.question: Symptoms with less-than-ordinary activity but comfort at rest correspond to {{c1::NYHA class III}}.

cards.explanation: Physical activity adds discomfort in the table’s most severe functional class.
cards.text: Heart-failure symptoms present even at rest correspond to {{c1::NYHA class IV}}.
cards.question: Heart-failure symptoms present even at rest correspond to {{c1::NYHA class IV}}.

cards.explanation: This is the named symptom beneath the functional-class table; distinguish it from orthopnoea when lying flat.
cards.text: Episodes of breathlessness that wake a patient at night are termed {{c1::paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea}}.
cards.question: Episodes of breathlessness that wake a patient at night are termed {{c1::paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea}}.

cards.explanation: The slide’s older three-drug “routine combination” is not a complete contemporary HFrEF algorithm; later slides also discuss MRAs, ARNI and SGLT2 inhibitors.
cards.text: HF treatment aims to improve symptoms and reduce hospitalisation while improving {{c1::survival}}.
cards.question: HF treatment aims to improve symptoms and reduce hospitalisation while improving {{c1::survival}}.

cards.explanation: Their site is the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle.
cards.text: Furosemide and bumetanide inhibit {{c1::Na+/K+/2Cl− cotransport}}.
cards.question: Furosemide and bumetanide inhibit {{c1::Na+/K+/2Cl− cotransport}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture gives hydrochlorothiazide and bendroflumethiazide as examples.
cards.text: Thiazide diuretics inhibit Na+/Cl− cotransport in the {{c1::distal convoluted tubule}}.
cards.question: Thiazide diuretics inhibit Na+/Cl− cotransport in the {{c1::distal convoluted tubule}}.

cards.explanation: This is distinct from direct epithelial sodium-channel inhibition.
cards.text: Spironolactone and eplerenone antagonise the {{c1::mineralocorticoid (aldosterone) receptor}}.
cards.question: Spironolactone and eplerenone antagonise the {{c1::mineralocorticoid (aldosterone) receptor}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture places this action in the late distal nephron/collecting duct.
cards.text: Amiloride and triamterene inhibit {{c1::epithelial sodium channels (ENaC)}}.
cards.question: Amiloride and triamterene inhibit {{c1::epithelial sodium channels (ENaC)}}.

cards.explanation: Their targets differ despite this shared electrolyte effect.
cards.text: Aldosterone antagonists and ENaC inhibitors are both {{c1::potassium-sparing}}.
cards.question: Aldosterone antagonists and ENaC inhibitors are both {{c1::potassium-sparing}}.

cards.explanation: Their benefit is not limited to mild sodium clearance.
cards.text: Mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonists also oppose aldosterone-mediated cardiac {{c1::fibrosis}}.
cards.question: Mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonists also oppose aldosterone-mediated cardiac {{c1::fibrosis}}.

cards.explanation: It improves pulmonary/peripheral oedema; symptom relief and evidence for mortality reduction are distinct outcomes.
cards.text: Diuresis reduces congestion by decreasing extracellular fluid volume and {{c1::preload}}.
cards.question: Diuresis reduces congestion by decreasing extracellular fluid volume and {{c1::preload}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture gives enalapril and valsartan as examples.
cards.text: ACE inhibition or AT1 blockade reduces vasoconstriction and therefore {{c1::afterload}}.
cards.question: ACE inhibition or AT1 blockade reduces vasoconstriction and therefore {{c1::afterload}}.

cards.explanation: Lower blood volume helps unload the failing heart.
cards.text: Reducing angiotensin-II/aldosterone signalling reduces sodium and {{c1::water retention}}.
cards.question: Reducing angiotensin-II/aldosterone signalling reduces sodium and {{c1::water retention}}.

cards.explanation: The negative acute inotropic effect does not negate its longer-term benefit in appropriately selected, stable patients.
cards.text: Evidence-based β-blockade in chronic HFrEF counters persistent {{c1::sympathetic overactivity}}.
cards.question: Evidence-based β-blockade in chronic HFrEF counters persistent {{c1::sympathetic overactivity}}.

cards.explanation: Bisoprolol is β1-selective. Do not assume every listed β-blocker has interchangeable mortality evidence in HFrEF.
cards.text: Carvedilol blocks β receptors and also {{c1::α1-adrenoceptors}}.
cards.question: Carvedilol blocks β receptors and also {{c1::α1-adrenoceptors}}.

cards.explanation: This is a supervised prescribing principle, not a self-adjustment instruction.
cards.text: The lecture advises beginning HF β-blocker treatment at a {{c1::low dose with gradual titration}}.
cards.question: The lecture advises beginning HF β-blocker treatment at a {{c1::low dose with gradual titration}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture lists atenolol alongside agents such as bisoprolol and carvedilol; avoid transferring mortality evidence indiscriminately across the class.
cards.text: A β-blocker’s inclusion in a lecture list does not mean all β-blockers have identical {{c1::HFrEF outcome evidence}}.
cards.question: A β-blocker’s inclusion in a lecture list does not mean all β-blockers have identical {{c1::HFrEF outcome evidence}}.

cards.explanation: The resulting sodium-gradient change reduces calcium extrusion via NCX.
cards.text: Digoxin inhibits the cardiac {{c1::Na+/K+-ATPase}}.
cards.question: Digoxin inhibits the cardiac {{c1::Na+/K+-ATPase}}.

cards.explanation: This is the positive inotropic mechanism shown for digoxin.
cards.text: Reduced NCX-mediated calcium extrusion increases intracellular calcium and {{c1::contractility}}.
cards.question: Reduced NCX-mediated calcium extrusion increases intracellular calcium and {{c1::contractility}}.

cards.explanation: It also lists persistent symptoms despite optimal treatment; not every patient with HF requires it.
cards.text: The lecture identifies HF with rapid {{c1::atrial fibrillation}} as a context where digoxin may be considered.
cards.question: The lecture identifies HF with rapid {{c1::atrial fibrillation}} as a context where digoxin may be considered.

cards.explanation: This contrasts with chronic β-blockade; positive inotropes have different clinical settings.
cards.text: Dobutamine is a β-adrenoceptor {{c1::agonist}}.
cards.question: Dobutamine is a β-adrenoceptor {{c1::agonist}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture links this to increased contractility.
cards.text: Milrinone inhibits phosphodiesterase, increasing {{c1::cAMP}}.
cards.question: Milrinone inhibits phosphodiesterase, increasing {{c1::cAMP}}.

cards.explanation: It is a calcium sensitiser, not the same target as digoxin.
cards.text: Levosimendan increases the calcium sensitivity of {{c1::troponin C}}.
cards.question: Levosimendan increases the calcium sensitivity of {{c1::troponin C}}.

cards.explanation: The drug lowers rate rather than acting as a direct positive inotrope.
cards.text: Ivabradine slows the sinoatrial node by inhibiting {{c1::If channels}}.
cards.question: Ivabradine slows the sinoatrial node by inhibiting {{c1::If channels}}.

cards.explanation: Mechanism refresher: the supplied CAD lecture, p. 20, explains how venous dilation reduces filling pressure.
cards.text: Venodilation by nitrates reduces ventricular {{c1::preload}}.
cards.question: Venodilation by nitrates reduces ventricular {{c1::preload}}.

cards.explanation: This explains how an arterial vasodilator such as the listed hydralazine can unload the failing ventricle.
cards.text: Arteriolar dilation lowers ventricular {{c1::afterload}}.
cards.question: Arteriolar dilation lowers ventricular {{c1::afterload}}.

cards.explanation: This reduces glucose reabsorption and increases urinary glucose excretion; HF benefit is not restricted to patients with diabetes.
cards.text: Dapagliflozin inhibits renal {{c1::SGLT2}}.
cards.question: Dapagliflozin inhibits renal {{c1::SGLT2}}.

cards.explanation: Reduced peptide degradation increases activity of natriuretic peptides.
cards.text: Sacubitril inhibits {{c1::neprilysin}}.
cards.question: Sacubitril inhibits {{c1::neprilysin}}.

cards.explanation: It provides the ARB component of sacubitril/valsartan.
cards.text: Valsartan blocks the {{c1::AT1 receptor}}.
cards.question: Valsartan blocks the {{c1::AT1 receptor}}.

cards.explanation: The complementary actions enhance beneficial peptide signalling while limiting angiotensin-II effects.
cards.text: Sacubitril/valsartan combines neprilysin inhibition with {{c1::angiotensin-receptor blockade}}.
cards.question: Sacubitril/valsartan combines neprilysin inhibition with {{c1::angiotensin-receptor blockade}}.

slides.topic: Heart Failure — Mechanisms & Drug Treatment — page 2
slides.text:
Heart Failure
Cardiac output (CO) is inadequate to meet the metabolic demands 
of the body
Causes:
Ischaemic heart disease/ Myocardial infarction 
Cardiomyopathies (any condition that cause defect of heart muscle )
Chronic hypertension
Abnormal valves – congenital defects, aortic or mitral valve stenosis,   regurgitation   
Myocarditis, pericarditis, endocarditis 
Metabolic disease eg/ thyrotoxicosis, Dabetes
Acute HF- sudden loss of cardiac function (eg due to myocardial 
infarction)
Chronic HF – progressive
~2% in under 50yrs, >10% in over 65yrs
High mortality - accounts for ~4% of all deaths in UK.
5 year survival rate around 45%

slides.topic: Heart Failure — Mechanisms & Drug Treatment — page 13
slides.text:
Drug treatment of HF
Routine combination of drugs: Diuretic + ACEI + Beta blocker
• Diuretics  
• RAAS inhibitors (ACEI or ARB)
• Beta blockers
• Positive inotropic drugs
• Vasodilators eg nitrates
• Ivabradine
• Sacubitril/valsartan
• sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors 
Aims: Improve symptoms , improve quality of ife
           reduce hospitalisation
           increase survival and life span

slides.topic: Heart Failure — Mechanisms & Drug Treatment — page 14
slides.text:
Thiazide diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide, bendroflumethiazide)
•
 Inhibits the Na+/Cl- co-transporter in the distal convoluted tubule
•
 Can be used as an adjunct
Loop diuretics (Furosemide, Bumetanide) 
•
Inhibit the Na+/K+/2Cl- co-transporter in the thick Ascending Limb of loop of Henle
•
Powerful, rapid fluid removal
Diuretics
Aldosterone Receptor Antagonists (Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists) 
(Spironolactone, Eplerenone)
•
Blocks action of aldosterone
•
Mild sodium clearance 
•
K+ sparing.
•
Block aldosterone's ability to cause cardiac fibrosis (scarring and stiffening of the heart 
tissue)
Epithelial Sodium Channel (ENaC) Inhibitors  (Amiloride, Triamterene)
•
Late Distal Tubule and Collecting Duct
•
K+ sparing

 A. they reduce fluid volume
